title: CoRL26 connected research atlas
source_policy: Concepts connect the available original CoRL talk transcripts with reviewed primary project pages and indexed paper sections. Each reference records reading depth; unread pointers remain visibly distinct. Company and empirical results remain attributed to their original authors. Social posts are not cited as research evidence.

references.title: Code as Policies: Language Model Programs for Embodied Control
references.summary: Code-writing language models translate instructions into executable robot programs that process perception outputs and call control APIs. This is a concrete example of writing the policy representation directly, rather than updating a neural policy through reinforcement learning.
references.verification: Primary manuscript text was read through the supported indexed-paper reader. Claims and limitations are paraphrases; benchmark figures are not treated as independently reproduced results.
references.source_origin: Meta CLI search.paper load: indexed public arXiv manuscript
references.mechanism: Few-shot examples → hierarchical Python generation → perception and control APIs → reactive loops or waypoint actions. Undefined helper functions can be generated recursively.
findings: The paper demonstrates tabletop manipulation, drawing and mobile-robot navigation/manipulation, including numerical spatial reasoning and unfamiliar instructions.
Its simulated tabletop evaluation separates unseen instructions from unseen attribute values, making the source of generalization more explicit.
limitations: The policy remains limited by available perception APIs and control primitives.
Cross-embodiment API adaptation is described as brittle; complex instructions outside the prompt examples can fail.
The method assumes feasible instructions and cannot establish the correctness of generated code before execution.
references.practical_takeaway: For a code-policy branch, show the API boundary and the validation step. A generated loop can change behavior without any neural weight update.

connections.why: Hang Zhao distinguishes code-produced control logic from learned motor policies across physical time scales.
ASPIRE combines retained code skills with GR00T control; this paper explains the code-policy representation, not ASPIRE’s measured performance.

references.title: GR00T 2: Scaling Robot Foundation Models for Generalization, Dexterity, and Adaptation
references.summary: GR00T 2 is a world-action model that jointly predicts future video and robot actions. Its official material separates three improvement mechanisms: policy post-training and real-world RL, an execution agent invoking the WAM API, and ASPIRE-authored code recovery skills. The agent watches for stalls, calls a code skill to repair the scene, then hands control back. Turbo compresses the video representation and model for onboard execution, with SONIC providing faster whole-body control.
references.verification: Primary project methods and evaluation text read on 2026-11-22; performance claims remain author-reported.
references.source_origin: Public search result and existing atlas link

The page also reports limits of visual steering: marks do not encode final object orientation or all motion, and some long tasks still rarely complete.

references.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5: Accelerating Physical Intelligence
references.summary: Gemini Robotics 2.5 is the robot action model; Gemini Robotics ER tracks workflow in the described automotive-kitting pilot. Gemini 4 Argon acts elsewhere in the development loop, building simulation practice data and helping diagnose rollout failures. These roles make this a useful concrete example of combining action execution, high-level supervision and agent-assisted learning.
references.verification: Primary project methods and evaluation text read on 2026-11-22; performance claims remain author-reported.
references.limitations: The company post reports task breadth, dexterity and a factory proof-of-concept; it does not supply independent verification or demonstrate unconstrained generalist deployment. The factory result is a particular kitting workflow, not a measured rate across all robot work.

references.title: GRAIL: Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models
references.summary: GRAIL grounds video generation in known 3D assets before reconstruction: geometry, cameras, metric scale and a robot-proportioned character are fixed inputs. Recovered human-object interaction is retargeted to a humanoid, then object-aware and scene-aware trackers convert it into robot-action data for downstream visual policy learning. This is a generated-training-data pipeline, rather than the robot performing online search in a video model.
references.verification: Primary project methods and evaluation text read on 2026-11-22; performance claims remain author-reported.
references.source_origin: Public search result and existing atlas link
references.limitations: Privileged scene information simplifies reconstruction and avoids the assumptions of unconstrained in-the-wild video recovery. Physical transfer examples are particular pickup and stair tasks; broad generation capability is not automatically broad deployed autonomy.

references.title: RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies
references.summary: RoboTTT integrates test-time-training layers into a robot policy. Their fast weights are fixed-size recurrent state: incoming tokens update those weights, and the updated state conditions actions. Sequence action forcing and truncated backpropagation enable long-sequence training. DAgger Distillation uses mistakes as context and corrections as action targets, giving a mechanism for within-episode recovery.
references.verification: Primary project methods and evaluation text read on 2026-11-22; performance claims remain author-reported.
references.limitations: Fast weights and persistent trained parameters play different roles. The reviewed assembly evaluations demonstrate context-dependent behavior; they do not establish that slow policy weights continually update across real deployments.

references.title: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model
references.summary: SuperMimic learns one differentiable world model of shared humanoid dynamics and jointly trains a tracking policy through imagined short rollouts. Gradients pass through the learned model rather than the rigid-body simulator. Its main contribution is amortizing this learning across a motion library, giving a practical alternative to repeatedly training specialists or using cluster-scale model-free RL.
references.verification: Indexed paper abstract and primary project method/evaluation text read; full indexed paper methods were unavailable on 2026-11-22; performance claims remain author-reported.
references.limitations: The official project page states that benchmark motions are training motions for both methods, so failure counts measure coverage, not generalization. Comparisons also use different GPU hardware and motion-data amounts; the report distinguishes return, wall time and GPU-hours.

references.title: DreamZero: World Action Models are Zero-shot Policies
references.summary: DreamZero learns a policy from a pretrained video-diffusion backbone by jointly predicting video and actions. Its official page separates novel task/environment tests, task-specific post-training, and new-embodiment adaptation with play data. Runtime optimization, asynchronous inference and smoothing are part of deploying the model, alongside the learning recipe.
references.limitations: “Zero-shot” is conditioned on the test axis. New embodiment adaptation uses target-robot play data, then tests novel tasks or objects; it is not strict no-target-exposure transfer. The reviewed page describes its own real-robot comparisons, and a visual rollout gallery does not replace a matched benchmark protocol.
references.verification: Primary project method and evaluation text read on 2026-11-22; empirical findings remain author-reported.

references.title: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
references.summary: The Argon primary post gives distinct examples of robot-control primitives, physically calibrated Real2Sim, hindsight annotation, simulation-generated training experience and iterative hardware repair. Its simulation reconstruction example separately checks visual match and force/torque timing, magnitude and direction. This makes the agent-run learning branch concrete: an agent can create experiments and accepted code/data artifacts without every example implying neural-weight learning.
references.limitations: The examples are company demonstrations with supplied prompts, hardware primitives and verification objectives. The iterative pick-and-place example improves an execution artifact; the simulation-data example supports a VLA training loop. Neither demonstrates recursive self-improvement of the underlying model or unlimited autonomy.

references.title: π0.7: A Steerable Generalist Robotic Foundation Model with Emergent Capabilities
references.summary: π0.7 diversifies the conditioning context, including subtask instructions, subgoal images, control modes and episode metadata. This lets a single model learn from demonstrations, suboptimal autonomous trajectories including failures, and non-robot sources while giving users more ways to specify desired behavior. The paper evaluates instruction following, cross-embodiment transfer and compositional tasks.
references.limitations: The authors explicitly say large, diverse data makes definitive seen-versus-unseen task classification difficult: related skills can appear under other labels or incidentally. Treat its out-of-the-box demonstrations as evidence under its data assumptions, and compare strict embodiment holdout separately.
references.verification: Indexed paper method, evaluation and discussion sections read on 2026-11-22; empirical findings remain author-reported.

references.title: FlowEval: How Much Adaptation Does an Embodied Foundation Model Need at Deployment?
references.summary: FlowEval uses a small set of successful target-domain demonstrations and the flow-matching objective to diagnose model–deployment fit without training. It probes predictive agreement and studies whether the score correlates with improvement as adaptation data is added. It supplies a useful decision layer before collecting another large dataset: diagnose what adaptation may remain, then test that prediction.
references.limitations: The method applies to flow-matching action models. It assumes actual rollout demonstrations with the issued action targets; post-hoc reconstructed action targets can invalidate the metric. The paper identifies calibrated predictions of the exact amount of data needed as future work, so correlation is not a guaranteed data-budget estimate.
references.verification: Indexed paper method, adaptation experiments and stated limitations read on 2026-11-22; empirical findings remain author-reported.

references.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
references.summary: VLRLA conditions actions on accumulated observations, actions, rewards and termination signals while keeping deployed model parameters fixed. Its in-context RL module learns during training how to use interaction history; deployment then changes the history rather than optimizing the checkpoint. The paper includes simulation studies and real tasks with cross-episode reward memory.
references.limitations: Fixed weights do not mean fixed behavior, but this is still distinct from persistent weight adaptation. Its histories and reward feedback are designed inputs, and the reported transfer is bounded by the evaluated tasks and training-history construction strategies.
references.verification: Indexed paper design, simulation and real-experiment sections read on 2026-11-22; empirical findings remain author-reported.

references.title: Dual-Stream Memory for Vision-Language-Action Policies
references.summary: Dual-Stream Memory separates compressed execution-stage context from selective access to historical visual detail. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet produces a compact temporal token; a task-conditioned retriever keeps relevant frames with spatial detail. This refines the memory question from “how long a context?” to “which information should be compressed, and which must remain accessible?”.
references.limitations: The paper reports non-additive benefits and task regressions, and real gains concentrate on repeated actions. Real checkpoints are matched by training loss rather than equal training steps. The authors call for matched full-system ablations and broader task/hardware tests, especially identity tracking through cup swaps.
references.verification: Indexed paper method, full-benchmark comparison and real-robot evaluation read on 2026-11-22; empirical findings remain author-reported.

references.title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
references.summary: ODE Policy learns a vector field for how robot commands evolve in physical time, then integrates it to produce an action trajectory. This is different from the denoising time of a generative flow head. The paper studies seamless chunk joins, small perturbations near demonstrations and a diversity head, with comparisons in imitation learning, VLA/WAM action heads and humanoid reinforcement learning.
references.limitations: The reported protocols use specific chunk lengths, integrators and control rates. Some execution-quality measures compare only successful episodes, while one real-task baseline measure comes from failures. The paper’s uses for arbitrary control rates and action-free learning include preliminary directions rather than finished solutions.
references.verification: Indexed paper method, experimental setup and future-directions sections read on 2026-11-22; empirical findings remain author-reported.

references.title: Early Warning Signals for OpenVLA Failure under Visual Distribution Shift
references.summary: Small monitors trained on internal OpenVLA activations can detect approaching failure under controlled visual occlusion. The useful distinction is between a predictive warning signal and a recovery action that actually makes the robot safer.
references.mechanism: Closed-loop rollout activations → fitted linear risk probe → calibrated warning threshold → runtime warning policy. The study compares the probe with a mean-difference direction and action-disagreement baseline.
findings: The strongest reported probe is at layer 16 among layers 8, 10 and 16, under the studied occlusion distribution.
Transfer to camera jitter is weaker; a strong score on one perturbation does not establish robustness across tasks and shifts.
limitations: The experimental setup uses five LIBERO-10 task IDs with a limited rollout budget.
Neighboring rollout states are correlated; the authors explicitly treat their result as controlled-setting decodability and call for episode-grouped and task-held-out evaluation.
A warning score alone is not a recovery policy; no-op, abort and held-action interventions are diagnostics.
references.practical_takeaway: Record both failure prediction and what happens after the warning. Use episode-separated evaluation and measure false alarms, lead time and successful recovery.

connections.why: Connects Burgard’s uncertainty and reliability questions to calibration, warning rate and the distinction between detection and intervention.
The contact-rich failure talk examines physical-control failures; this preprint studies visual-shift warnings. These failure classes should remain separate.

references.title: HandEdit: A Unified Benchmark for Egocentric Human-to-Robot Dexterous Hand Image Editing
references.summary: HandEdit studies how to replace a human hand in egocentric footage with a target robotic embodiment while preserving the object interaction. It provides a sharper evaluation lens for human-to-robot synthetic data: realistic pixels are insufficient if morphology or contact is wrong.
references.mechanism: Egocentric hand-object data → retargeted/rendered robot-embodied pseudo-references → image editing → separate perceptual, semantic and embodiment-aware evaluation.
findings: The benchmark separates hand-only editing from the harder hand-and-arm editing setting.
Its analysis finds that high perceptual quality or a high VLM judgment score need not imply correct embodiment structure or preserved interaction.
limitations: Pixel-aligned human and robot pairs cannot be physically captured in identical configurations; edited pseudo-references retain appearance and contact-dynamics gaps.
The authors state that this data supports pretraining and mid-training and does not replace real-robot demonstrations.
The benchmark evaluates image editing; downstream control benefit requires separate robot-policy evidence.

references.title: ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World
references.review_scope: The indexed manuscript yielded only title/abstract. The complete primary project page was read, including the four-module method, physical reset/evaluation examples, policy-improvement regimes, fleet experiments and stated limitations. Full manuscript methods were not available through the indexed reader.
references.full_summary: ENPIRE makes selected physical manipulation tasks accessible to coding agents as repeatable research environments. Its Environment component resets scenes and verifies outcomes; Policy Improvement launches a chosen refinement routine; Rollout evaluates candidates on one or more robots; Evolution lets coding agents inspect failures and modify algorithm or infrastructure code. The improvement interface accepts several regimes, including heuristics, code/tool use, behavior cloning, offline RL and online RL. Consequently, the changed artifact can be an executable program, a training recipe or a learned policy, depending on the experiment. The project describes agent-run iterations on prepared tasks such as Push-T and pin insertion, together with simulation experiments and fleet-resource measurements. This is evidence of an engineered loop around real interaction, rather than merely a supervisor choosing skills during one episode. Its autonomy claim is scoped to the provided self-resetting, self-verifying task interfaces. The site labels its showcased 99% result as pass@8, so it should not be rewritten as single-attempt reliability. All results remain author-reported.
references.method: Expose reset, observation, action and reward APIs for a prepared task. Coding agents propose changes, launch the selected PI regime, collect real rollouts, inspect success and failure evidence, then retain useful changes. Multiple agents can explore branches in parallel while robot and compute utilization are monitored. When PI invokes RL or behavior cloning, a learning routine updates policy parameters; when it uses heuristic code, the improvement is in the program. Both fit the same harness but are different learning artifacts.
references.why_it_matters: It gives the agentic panel a concrete physical policy-improvement system, and gives the training panel an example that can choose among code changes, demonstrations and RL. Reset and verification engineering are part of what makes that automation possible.
references.open_question: How much of the improvement survives new task setups and imperfect reset or reward verification, and what is the full cost of preparing the physical environment rather than only running the agent loop?
limitations: The demonstrated autonomy assumes task-specific automatic reset, perception, reward verification and available robot-control tools; it is not evidence of autonomous setup for arbitrary robots or tasks.
The primary page reports 99% pass@8 on showcased tasks. That metric permits repeated attempts and is not a single-rollout success guarantee.
The authors report robot underutilization while agents read, debug or wait, and rising token consumption as fleets and coordinating agents scale.
This review used substantive primary project text plus an indexed abstract, not a complete primary manuscript-method review.

references.title: HARBOR: A Harness Framework for Agentic Robot Reinforcement Learning
references.review_scope: Indexed manuscript main methods, experiments, real-world validation, ablations and stated limitations were read. Primary project guide was also read to corroborate the harness design. Indexed equations/tables contain formatting loss, so extracted table values are not used for headline comparisons; appendices were not reviewed exhaustively.
references.full_summary: HARBOR automates the engineering workflow surrounding robot reinforcement learning in simulation. A central agent divides a request into bounded stages such as dependencies, task construction, rewards, domain randomization, RL integration and tuning. Stage-local agents operate through standard commands and persistent artifacts. Executable gates check interfaces and rollout evidence before later stages proceed; failures are repaired within a retry budget and unresolved stages can require human intervention. Reward and hyperparameter candidates run in isolated parallel trials, while an experience ledger preserves useful heuristics and failure diagnoses for later runs. This separates the coding agent that constructs or tunes the experiment from the numerical RL algorithm that trains the policy. The authors evaluate multiple simulation backends and include physical validation, but the latter uses user-provided real trajectories, interface engineering and human feedback for simulator alignment. The source explicitly warns that gates do not guarantee semantic policy correctness. Its results support a scoped engineering-automation claim, not a general guarantee that any agent can autonomously train reliable real-world policies.
references.method: Persist workflow state as code, configuration, logs, videos and checkpoints. Delegate each bounded stage to an isolated agent, run standard commands, and admit outputs only after executable interface or rollout checks. Parallelize iterative reward/algorithm trials, aggregate their outcomes, then write reusable lessons into an experience store. Standard RL training carries out parameter learning. Sim-to-real alignment adds measured trajectories, system identification and human feedback; it is not automatically solved by passing simulation gates.
references.why_it_matters: It makes agentic learning operational: the agent engineers experiments while RL performs policy optimization. The persistent-artifact and gate design also shows what must be inspected when an automated pipeline reports success.
references.open_question: How robust is the harness on unfamiliar tasks without supplied templates or expert heuristics, and how much practical effort remains in physical interfaces and simulator alignment after simulation training succeeds?
limitations: Executable gates catch particular engineering failures but do not prove that the reward captures the intended behavior or that the final policy is semantically correct.
The authors explicitly retain manual robot-interface engineering, user-provided real trajectories and human feedback at the sim-to-real boundary.
The evaluated policies are relatively simple; extending the framework to VLA or world-model policies is described as future work.
Some reward-design gains rely on supplied human heuristics and accumulated experience. Their contribution should remain visible when comparing automation methods.

references.title: MobiAgent: Dual-Loop Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
references.review_scope: Primary manuscript introduction, inner/outer-loop methods, main experiments and conclusion/limitations were read, together with the complete primary project page and reported deployment-round tables. Detailed supplementary prompts and all appendix failure cases were not exhaustively reviewed.
references.full_summary: MobiAgent separates deployment-time planning from offline policy refinement. Its inner loop uses a VLM planner, a shared VLM trunk with skill-specific flow-matching action experts, and a reflection critic that recommends advance, retry or replan. Critic observations are retained as episode memory. The outer loop runs after episode termination: it segments and verifies trajectories, standardizes skill captions and trains or fine-tunes neural skill policies. Startup data creates the skill inventory; subsequent rollout data is assigned to the existing inventory, and the described continual phase updates those existing policies without expanding the model inventory. This is more specific than saying the robot simply learns through reasoning or that its skill vocabulary grows without bound. The authors report finite deployment-to-training rounds on RoboCasa and Astribot S1, plus long-horizon BEHAVIOR tasks. Early RoboCasa gains later plateau. Here the reusable changes are learned skill policies and curated data; the paper does not establish indefinite improvement or a learning procedure that recursively redesigns itself.
references.method: A task planner combines current observations, episode memory and skill names into the next subtask. A chosen flow-matching expert executes action chunks; a visual critic decides whether to advance, retry or replan. After an episode, separate curation verifies skill clips. Startup captions are clustered to create canonical skills, but rollout clips are mapped to those established skills. references.title: PhysCaP: Grounding Code-as-Policy Agent with Physics-Informed Exploration
references.review_scope: Primary arXiv v2 main text through methods, real/simulation experiments, discussion and conclusion/limitations was read; primary project page and workshop publication note were also read. ARK returned a mismatched HPC-paper body under this title, which was rejected and not used. Appendices were not reviewed comprehensively.
references.full_summary: PhysCaP gives a code-as-policy agent explicit ways to acquire physical information that an image alone may not reveal. Training-free modules estimate object mass using differential joint torque during a lift and stiffness using gripper force-displacement measurements. A Planner decides what information is missing and when exploration can stop; a Prioritizer filters and orders candidate interactions; a coding agent produces programs that call measurement and control APIs. Measurements update a task belief before further exploration or execution. The evaluated improvement is therefore in information gathering and programmatic control, rather than a new neural policy trained online. The study reports three physical tabletop tasks and a simulated hidden-mass task, with component comparisons that distinguish having measurement tools from choosing efficient interactions. Interaction-count and execution-time statistics are conditional on successful episodes. Simulation exposes a mass-sensing API only after a verified lift. These conditions are important when interpreting comparisons with passive policies; the experiments do not establish that all VLAs lack active perception or that the agent can infer arbitrary physics.
references.method: Use existing proprioception to estimate mass from loaded-versus-empty grasp torque and stiffness from gripper force/displacement. The Planner proposes needed measurements and a stopping decision; the Prioritizer ranks feasible candidate interactions from visual/task cues. A coding agent invokes the measurement APIs and robot-control primitives. The measured values enter belief storage and guide the next plan. No additional physical-property model training is required by these modules, although their perception and hardware interfaces remain assumptions of the setup.
references.why_it_matters: It makes a useful boundary case for the panels: a robot can improve decisions by measuring and rewriting control programs without changing neural policy weights. The relevant artifact is a better-grounded belief and executable plan.
references.open_question: How reliable are the measurement and exploration choices for unfamiliar materials, geometry and hardware, especially when value comes from avoided failed episodes rather than efficiency measured only on successes?
limitations: The implementation estimates a narrow set of physical quantities with particular robot/gripper measurements; it is not a general physical-property inference system.
Object interactions and execution time are reported only for successful episodes. Lower interaction counts alone do not establish better overall success or cost.

references.title: ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics
references.review_scope: Primary arXiv v2 introduction, execution-engine/skill-library/evolutionary-search methods, curriculum and backward transfer, main evaluation protocol, zero-shot/real-robot studies, ablations and stated limitations were read. Detailed appendix prompts and all per-task results were not reviewed exhaustively.
references.full_summary: ASPIRE learns robot control programs and reusable repair knowledge while keeping its underlying LLM frozen. Its execution engine exposes per-primitive multimodal traces so an actor can locate failures in perception, planning, grasping or control. Evolutionary search explores several candidate programs using debug seeds. Validated repairs are proposed as compact skill guidance containing a failure signature, when-to-apply condition, repair strategy and sometimes a code sketch. A fresh verifier actor checks a proposed skill on its source task before admission, and later actors retrieve the library as context. The learned artifact is thus executable code and persistent repair guidance, not an online update to the LLM’s neural weights. Evaluation separates debug and held-out seeds, with distinct procedures for different benchmarks. Simulation-discovered skills help real-robot debugging, but the paper explicitly says transfer is not direct policy deployment. The real cube study still uses human task guidance, scrambling and scene resets. One-time skill admission also leaves stale or misleading entries as an unresolved scaling issue.
references.method: An actor writes and executes a robot program, inspects primitive-level traces, then repairs the program or proposes diverse candidates. Search selects programs on debug seeds within a round budget. The actor summarizes potentially reusable repairs; a separate verifier attempts the source task and the coordinator admits reusable API-compliant entries. Future actors use those entries as in-context guidance. Curriculum selection and a bounded rerun of earlier low-performing tasks provide opportunities for backward transfer. The main policy representation is code plus text skill knowledge.
references.why_it_matters: It deepens the original skill-discovery perspective with explicit artifacts, admission checks and held-out protocols. It also prevents conflating code-space continual learning with neural-weight training or fully autonomous real-world lifelong learning.
references.open_question: How should accumulated skills be revalidated, pruned and retrieved when tasks or robot APIs change, and how much human reset/calibration work is needed beyond the showcased real-robot experiments?
limitations: The underlying LLM is frozen, and its strength plus the predefined perception/planning/control API bounds expressible behavior.

references.title: EmbodiedSWE: Coding Agents for Long Horizon Dexterous Robotics
references.review_scope: Primary arXiv v2 benchmark design, solver protocol, task/embodiment transfer, supporting-tool study, demonstration-generation methods, VLA training/generalization experiments, real-robot transfer and Appendix I limitations were read. Complete appendix implementation/prompt/result listings were not reviewed exhaustively.
references.full_summary: EmbodiedSWE separates coding agents as task solvers from coding agents as sources of policy supervision. Its benchmark contains human-designed long-horizon, contact-rich simulation tasks. Agents inspect privileged simulator state and iteratively produce executable solution programs; an isolated grader checks submitted artifacts. Verified solutions then seed EmbodiedSWE-Gen, which diversifies scenes, strategies, intermediate phases and perturbations, retaining trajectories after grader and replay checks. Those demonstrations fine-tune VLAs, so the resulting neural policy update is distinct from the coding agent’s program search. The authors test data scaling and held-out variations, and show a real four-stage lamp-disassembly example trained only on generated simulation demonstrations. That physical result covers one task and ten trials, with limited full-task completion. Appendix I also distinguishes these component studies from a broader synthetic-task-generation-to-policy pipeline that has not been run end to end. A separate exploratory RL post-training experiment for the coding agent lacks held-out checkpoint evaluation. The work provides a useful teacher-data route, not proof that all coding-agent capability has already been distilled into a general robot.
references.method: First let a coding agent build a successful program against a fixed simulated task. Diversify the verified solution through changes to scene, strategy, task phases and noise, plus scripted physics/visual randomization. Admit generated trajectories only after task grading and replay checks. Train a VLA on those demonstrations and evaluate it separately. Program search can use checkpoint trees, parallel sweeps or CMA-ES over program parameters; those optimizations should not be mistaken for the later VLA’s weight training.
references.why_it_matters: It provides a source-backed distinction within the panels between writing a control program and learning a neural policy from the resulting experience. The teacher-data mechanism is explicit, with both held-out and limited physical evaluations.
references.open_question: How much coding-agent capability transfers through a fully automatic task-generation-to-policy pipeline, and do the generated visual/physical scenes support reliable transfer beyond the demonstrated real task?
limitations: Coding-agent solver experiments use full simulator state, engineered control interfaces and human-designed tasks; their success is not a direct test of vision-only deployment autonomy.
The physical VLA transfer study covers one four-stage lamp task over ten trials, with 20% cumulative full completion; it should not become a general claim of reliable long-horizon real-robot control.
Appendix I says the broader synthetic-task construction, solution generation, diversification and policy-learning pipeline has not been studied end to end.
Exploratory RL post-training of the coding agent lacks held-out checkpoint evaluation, and broader dexterous-hand embodiments remain open questions.

references.full_summary: This study asks how a fixed demonstration budget should be distributed across instruction factors, rather than treating data scale as a single count. It deliberately correlates pairs of factors during fine-tuning, then evaluates held-out combinations to diagnose which factor a policy follows when cues conflict. references.full_summary: H2RBench compares human-to-robot transfer methods under a shared task and supervision protocol. references.title: RARA: Robust Policy Fine-Tuning through Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment for Robotic Manipulation

references.full_summary: RARA reuses selected pretraining demonstrations to guide task adaptation. It retrieves trajectories by instruction similarity, then matches target frames to relevant source phases by action-chunk similarity. First it trains representation-producing layers and a small projector to align target features with frozen pretrained features. It then behavior-clones the target task while constraining how the policy represents the retrieved source observations. references.full_summary: Memory Anchors studies which old experiences help a robot policy retain earlier tasks during sequential learning. It identifies new-task observations that overlap old-task representations but require different actions, then selects nearby old experiences for replay. references.title: FAR: Failure-Aware Retry for Test-Time Recovery and Continual Policy Improvement
references.review_scope: Primary manuscript main text, method (§4), experiments (§5), limitations (§6), and evaluation protocol (§C.3) read through the supported PDF-text reader; primary project page also read. Other appendix sections were not comprehensively reviewed.
references.full_summary: FAR addresses the case in which an existing diffusion policy fails and a naive retry repeats the same behavior. It uses critic estimates to select potentially failure-inducing action chunks, pairs them with higher-valued alternatives, and performs a short preference-based policy update before retrying. Smoothed action perturbations provide local exploration. A separate improvement loop combines expert data, successful online trajectories and failed trajectories: the critic learns from the collected experience, while the actor learns from expert and successful data. The reported evaluation covers nine simulated manipulation tasks and three real xArm tasks, with bounded retry budgets. The paper supports distinguishing immediate recovery from longer-term policy improvement, but its autonomy claim needs care: real experiments use a human’s binary success/failure signal, and the arm is returned to its initial configuration between retries while the scene remains changed. Tests use single-task diffusion policies trained from scratch; transfer to large pretrained VLAs and principled automatic failure detection are stated future work.

references.full_summary: ATOM-Bench separates learning elementary manipulation skills from recombining them under new task structures. references.title: ContactGuard: Pre-Contact Execution Monitoring with Action-Conditioned Latent World Models
references.review_scope: Indexed primary manuscript introduction, latent-model/probe methods, online monitor, experimental setup/results and limitations read. Figures and the complete original PDF were not independently inspected.
references.full_summary: ContactGuard is an execution monitor for a policy that proposes action chunks. It learns action-conditioned visual dynamics from unlabeled robot trajectories, freezes that latent world model, and trains a small failure probe on labeled pre-contact clips. Before a predicted gripper closure, the monitor rolls the model forward under the policy’s own planned actions and scores the future latent. A task-calibrated threshold can veto the chunk while the underlying policy remains unchanged. The experiments use four grasp settings on a dual-arm robot and compare future-latent monitoring against matched current-state and action-corruption controls. The live evaluation is a controlled counterfactual protocol: flagged attempts pause before contact and then resume so the would-be outcome can be recorded. Its claim is predictive abstention, not completed autonomous recovery or policy learning. The paper explicitly leaves post-abort completion and longer-horizon monitoring for future work. It therefore supports reporting false aborts, missed failures and subsequent task completion separately.

references.title: RLE-Bench: A Qualifying Exam for Coding Agents as Robot Learning Engineers
references.review_scope: Complete primary project overview and technical blog read, including nine task definitions, development budgets, hidden-evaluation protocols and case studies. The arXiv manuscript was not indexed, and the PDF reader did not return it. Dynamic aggregate score charts were not readable and are not treated as verified numeric results.
references.full_summary: RLE-Bench evaluates a coding agent’s robot-learning engineering process, not only the controller it finally produces. Nine tasks span interactive control, policy development, perception and estimation, and mechanical design. Depending on the task, the submitted artifact may be retained agent context, a harness for a fresh agent, an exported policy, a training recipe, an estimator or a mechanical design. The benchmark constrains development time, interactions and compute, then tests the result under hidden conditions. Its overview also distinguishes three interface levels: low-level APIs, reusable robotics tools, and privileged simulator state. These interfaces matter when interpreting agent comparisons. The public technical report includes cases in which visible objectives or development tests fail to predict broader checks, reinforcing the value of independently held-out evaluation. The benchmark does not establish field reliability for generalist robots: some transfer is explicitly sim-to-sim, aggregate charts were unreadable here, and reported API cost excludes simulation and GPU infrastructure.

references.why_it_matters: The artifact and evaluation boundary identify what an agent improved. An engineering score or a successful preview is not the same as a verified long-term robot deployment.

references.summary: RLE-Bench evaluates a coding agent’s robot-learning engineering process, not only the controller it finally produces. Nine tasks span interactive control, policy development, perception and estimation, and mechanical design. Depending on the task, the submitted artifact may be retained agent context, a harness for a fresh agent, an exported policy, a training recipe, an estimator or a mechanical design. The benchmark constrains development time, interactions and compute, then tests the result under hidden conditions. Its overview also distinguishes three interface levels: low-level APIs, reusable robotics tools, and privileged simulator state. These interfaces matter when interpreting agent comparisons. The public technical report includes cases in which visible objectives or development tests fail to predict broader checks, reinforcing the value of independently held-out evaluation. The benchmark does not establish field reliability for generalist robots: some transfer is explicitly sim-to-sim, aggregate charts were unreadable here, and reported API cost excludes simulation and GPU infrastructure.
references.verification: Complete primary project overview and technical blog read, including nine task definitions, development budgets, hidden-evaluation protocols and case studies. The arXiv manuscript was not indexed, and the PDF reader did not return it. Dynamic aggregate score charts were not readable and are not treated as verified numeric results. Results are author-reported; no independent reproduction is claimed.

references.title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs

references.full_summary: LeWAM jointly learns action-conditioned latent dynamics and a flow-matching action policy. The physical-robot experiments use direct policy execution; they do not demonstrate that online planning improves every physical task. references.open_question: Does the planning benefit survive unfamiliar objects, changing viewpoints and real-robot goal-conditioned tasks at a matched runtime budget?

references.title: Rolling-WAM: World Action Models with Rolling Imagination
references.review_scope: Indexed manuscript methods, training, benchmark protocols, real-robot evaluation and limitations, corroborated by the primary project page.
references.full_summary: Rolling-WAM distributes joint video-action denoising across successive control updates. It completes the next action chunk while retaining partially refined future chunks, then incorporates a new observation as the window advances. The paper evaluates simulation benchmarks and three Unitree G1 manipulation tasks. Its timing comparison measures steady-state replanning rather than startup or the complete robot lifecycle. The authors also identify a trade-off: retained future predictions can lag behind rapid scene changes, particularly with long windows.
references.method: Maintain a sliding video-action prediction window at staggered noise levels; finish, execute and replace the nearest chunk while refining its future continuation.
references.why_it_matters: Changes how prediction compute is allocated over time, supplying another concrete timing strategy alongside the conference discussion of robot control clocks.
references.open_question: How do window size and initialization cost affect response to abrupt changes outside the demonstrated task distribution?
limitations: Latency timing includes visual encoding and denoising but excludes warm-up and initialization.
The physical evaluation covers three manipulation tasks; it is not evidence of unrestricted humanoid generality.
Long prediction windows can preserve stale future context.

references.title: ImageWAM: Do World Action Models Really Need Video Generation, or Just Image Editing?
references.review_scope: Indexed manuscript architecture, objectives, inference, experiments and ablations, corroborated by the complete primary project page.
references.full_summary: ImageWAM attaches an action expert to an image-editing backbone. During inference it computes editing-aware attention context from one editing-branch step, then denoises an action chunk using that context. It does not decode a complete future image or generate a dense future video for each update. The study reports simulation benchmarks and four dual-arm hardware tasks, with multiple editing backbones. This supports examining how much visual prediction an action policy needs in those settings, rather than declaring video prediction unnecessary for all robot control.
references.method: Train the editing branch and action expert together, retain frozen understanding components, and use editing caches to condition action flow matching.
references.why_it_matters: Supplies a main-paper alternative to dense future-video intermediates and separates one editing-step shortcut from the remaining action-denoising computation.
references.open_question: Which dynamic or longer-horizon tasks require temporal prediction that an editing-cache intermediate does not retain?
limitations: A single editing-branch step is not a single-step action-generation or complete-control-loop guarantee.
Reported results cover the specified training, benchmark and hardware settings; generalized dominance is not established.
Different backbone variants and efficiency baselines use different interfaces, so figures should not be pooled without their protocols.

references.title: LaWAM: Latent World Action Models for Efficient Dynamics-Aware Robot Policies
references.review_scope: Indexed manuscript model stages, component ablations, physical-time alignment, real-robot protocols and limitations, corroborated by the complete primary project page.
references.full_summary: LaWAM learns a latent-action-conditioned world model in a frozen visual feature space, then teaches a language-conditioned policy to predict the latent action needed for a future subgoal. An action expert uses that compact future feature without rendering future pixels. The manuscript includes physical-time alignment for mixed-frequency action data and controlled task evaluations. Its stated limitations include unstable camera motion and insufficient coverage of fine deformable dynamics. Coherent open-loop latent rollouts on other embodiments are not the same evidence as successful closed-loop control on a new robot.
references.method: Pretrain latent dynamics, distill transition codes into a policy prior, and condition action chunks on a predicted latent visual subgoal.
references.why_it_matters: Connects predictive representation design with practical action timing, while identifying where future-state features and native action frequencies enter the policy.
references.open_question: Can its latent dynamics retain useful task change when camera self-motion or fine contact deformation dominates the observation?
limitations: The paper states a preference for relatively stable camera views and weaker modeling of rare fine-grained deformation.
Open-loop cross-embodiment latent visualization does not establish zero-shot closed-loop policy deployment on those robots.
